blocks.title: After this PDF you can
bullets: find the stem of a verb and make all present-tense forms
apply the spelling changes (maken → maak, leven → leef)
ask yes/no questions with the verb first (Werk je hier?)
talk about routines and about what is happening now

blocks.text: Take the infinitive (werken) and remove -en: that is the stem (werk). The stem is the form for ik; add -t for jij, u, hij, zij, het; and use the whole infinitive for all plural forms. That is all: Dutch has three forms where English has two.

blocks.text: The stem follows the spelling rule of pdf 1: a long vowel needs two letters in a closed syllable, a double consonant becomes single at the end, and a word never ends in v or z.

blocks.title: gaan, staan, doen, slaan, zien
blocks.text: These short verbs have a stem of one syllable: ik ga, jij gaat, wij gaan; ik sta; ik doe; ik sla; ik zie. And komen has ik kom, jij komt (with one o, against the rule).
Dutch needs no do. For a yes/no question, put the verb first: Werk je hier? (Do you work here?) With a question word, the verb comes right after it: Waar woon je? (Where do you live?)

blocks.title: Werk jij? — the t disappears after the verb
blocks.text: When jij / je follows the verb, the -t falls away: Jij werkt, but Werk jij? and Wat drink je? This happens only with jij and je, not with u or hij: Werkt u hier? Werkt hij hier?
4. One tense for 'I work' and 'I'm working'

The Dutch present tense covers both English present tenses: Ik lees = I read and I'm reading. To stress that something is happening right now, use zijn aan het + infinitive: Ik ben aan het koken (I'm cooking at the moment).

blocks.title: No 'I am working' word for word
blocks.text: Never translate I am working as Ik ben werken. Say Ik werk, or, for right now, Ik ben aan het werken. Dutch also uses the present for the future: Morgen werk ik thuis (I'm working at home tomorrow).

rows: After the verb, jij loses the -t.
A Dutch word never ends in v.
Closed syllable: long vowel with two letters.
Stem ends in t: no extra t.
No do in questions: verb first.
